name: Propantheline

lead: Propantheline is an older tablet that dermatology references list for excessive sweating, and people who want to stay dry and presentable look to it for that purpose.

It blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, reducing gland secretion and smooth muscle contraction. References group it with glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin as oral anticholinergics for focal and generalised hyperhidrosis, and it is also used for stomach and bladder spasm. No clinical trial of propantheline for sweating was identified; the literature concerns mainly bladder and gastric use.

paras: It is taken as a tablet under medical direction. Less sweating is the expected effect, alongside general gland drying.
Fast heart rate, constipation, light sensitivity, dry mouth, blurred vision and urinary retention are reported. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Propantheline is an older anticholinergic tablet that dermatology references list for excessive sweating, used by people who want drier skin and clothes. It blocks the signal that makes sweat glands secrete. Information on its sweat use comes mainly from reference listings rather than sweat trials.

lead: Propantheline bromide is an oral prescription antimuscarinic drug that blocks acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors in smooth muscle, glands and the eye. Dermatology references list it as one of several oral anticholinergics used for excessive sweating (hyperhidrosis), which gives it an appearance angle: less sweating means fewer visible sweat marks on clothing, drier hands and a more comfortable social presence [1][2][3]. A brand name is Pro-Banthine [1].

Hyperhidrosis is described as affecting up to 2.8 percent of the US population, and over 80 percent of patients report moderate to severe emotional effects, with avoidance of handshakes and visible sweat stains among the common concerns [2]. Treatment ladders usually begin with aluminium-based antiperspirants and move to iontophoresis, oral anticholinergics such as propantheline, glycopyrrolate and oxybutynin, botulinum toxin and surgery [2][3].

The published studies found for propantheline mainly concern bladder and gastric uses, such as a randomized comparison with oxybutynin for overactive bladder, a registered placebo-controlled study in overactive bladder, and pharmacokinetic work in healthy volunteers.[4][5][6][7] Hyperhidrosis references list it without citing a dedicated sweating trial. It is a prescription-only medicine.

paras: The appearance relevance of propantheline comes from hyperhidrosis. Excessive underarm sweating soaks clothing and can cause chafing and dermatitis, palmar sweating can lead to avoiding handshakes, and plantar sweating can cause odour and ruined footwear, according to DermNet [3]. Taking an anticholinergic before an anxiety-provoking event is described as an option in the hyperhidrosis literature [2].

Reference works list propantheline for hyperhidrosis, cramps and spasms of the stomach, intestines or bladder, involuntary urination (enuresis) and irritable-bowel-type symptoms. Dentists sometimes prescribe it to reduce excessive salivation [1]. Oral anticholinergics including propantheline, glycopyrrolate, oxybutynin, methantheline and benzatropine are described as treating both focal and generalised hyperhidrosis [2][3].

sections.h: Where it sits in hyperhidrosis care
paras: DermNet describes primary hyperhidrosis as affecting about 1 to 3 percent of the US population, usually starting in childhood or adolescence, and arranges treatment from least to most invasive: general measures and aluminium-based antiperspirants (10 to 25 percent), topical anticholinergics such as glycopyrronium cloths and oxybutynin gel, iontophoresis, oral anticholinergics, botulinum toxin injections, sweat-gland removal procedures and, for the most severe cases, sympathectomy.[3]

Oral options in that list include propantheline, oxybutynin and benztropine, with glycopyrrolate used off-label; beta-blockers and clonidine may help some patients.[3] DermNet notes that botulinum toxin is approved for armpit sweating and typically reduces sweating for three to six months, that iontophoresis is usually repeated daily for several weeks, and that sympathectomy can be followed by compensatory sweating at other sites.[3]

The impact described is practical and visible: damp, stained clothing needing frequent changes and chafing in the armpits, slippery palms that lead people to avoid handshakes or affect handwriting and keyboard use, and foot sweating that causes odour and damages footwear.[3]

Propantheline is an antispasmodic that blocks acetylcholine from acting on muscarinic receptors in smooth muscle in the gut, bladder and eye, and in secretory tissue. Because acetylcholine drives smooth muscle contraction and secretions, blocking it relaxes those muscles and reduces secretions such as sweat, saliva and tears [1]. A 1977 review of parasympathetic depressants places propantheline among the synthetic quaternary ammonium antimuscarinics alongside methantheline and others [8].

The only route listed is oral [1]. A 1979 study in the British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology examined the pharmacokinetics of propantheline bromide in normal men [9]. Propantheline has also been used in research as a tool to slow gastric emptying and gut motility when studying the absorption of other drugs [10].
Propantheline is a quaternary ammonium compound and a xanthene carboxylate ester supplied as the bromide salt, with a molar mass of about 368.5 g/mol [1].

Listed effects include fast heart rate, constipation, light sensitivity, dry mouth and urinary retention [1]. DermNet notes that dry mouth is common, that blurred vision, constipation, dizziness or palpitations occur less often, that oral anticholinergics are avoided in people with glaucoma or urinary retention, that older adults face higher risk of side effects including dementia, and that interactions with other medicines occur [3]. Dermatology references list the same pattern: dry mouth, urinary retention, constipation and vision changes [2].

Wikipedia also lists use for severe gastrointestinal symptoms during tapering off tricyclic antidepressants.[1] DermNet advises that oral anticholinergics should not be used by people with glaucoma or urinary retention and that they call for clinician review because of interactions.[3]

Overactive bladder. A randomized, double-blind, multicentre trial compared oxybutynin, propantheline and placebo for frequency, urgency and incontinence related to detrusor hyperactivity [4]. A Cochrane review examined anticholinergic drugs versus placebo for overactive bladder in adults [5]. A registered randomized, placebo-controlled study (NCT01640002, started 2012, n=42) assessed propantheline for overactive bladder associated with HTLV-1 [6].

Healthy-volunteer pharmacology. Propantheline was used to slow gastric emptying in absorption studies, including a 1979 Lancet study of gel fibre and absorption of glucose and paracetamol and studies of its effect on absorption of cimetidine [10][7].

Hyperhidrosis. No clinical trial of propantheline for sweating was identified. Wikipedia and DermNet list it among oral anticholinergics for the condition without citing a specific trial for the drug [2][3].

Newer options have joined the hyperhidrosis toolkit. In 2018 the FDA approved topical glycopyrronium tosylate cloths for underarm hyperhidrosis, and botulinum toxin is approved for underarm hyperhidrosis with effects lasting several months [2][3]. Social media coverage of hyperhidrosis was the subject of a 2024 analysis of TikTok content [11].

DermNet reports that primary hyperhidrosis is particularly common in Japanese people and may be inherited.[3] Wikipedia notes that its propantheline article needs more citations and does not address contraindications, dosing or history, and no drug-specific sweating trial is cited for it.[1]

timeline.event: FDA approves topical glycopyrronium tosylate for primary axillary hyperhidrosis, widening non-oral options for the condition [2].
